questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A hypothesis and the prediction it makes
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the numerical value a stated prediction implies
questions.stem: A transit planner predicts that adding a bus-only lane on a 6 km corridor will cut peak journey times by 12 percent within a year of opening. If the current mean peak journey time is 25 minutes, what peak journey time does the prediction give after the change?
questions.explanation: A 12 percent cut leaves 88 percent of 25 minutes, and 25 times 0.88 equals 22. Adding 12 minutes instead of scaling by 0.88 ignores that the change is proportional.
questions.hint: Multiply the current mean by the fraction that remains.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a result that could disprove a proposed mechanism

Average journey time on the corridor falls by nine minutes each weekday
options.misconception: mistakes an outcome for a test of the stated mechanism

options.text: The lane carries four buses per hour at peak instead of two
options.misconception: believes added capacity proves drivers changed behaviour

options.text: Signal offsets are retimed at six junctions along the corridor
options.misconception: treats carrying out the intervention as confirming it

questions.explanation: Flat ridership after retiming contradicts the predicted driver shift. Journey time, service frequency and retimed offsets are each compatible with the mechanism being true.
questions.hint: Pick the observation that contradicts the predicted shift.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Compare a modelled prediction with a field measurement
questions.stem: A planner's traffic model predicts 14 minutes for a 5 km trip at peak, but a GPS trace of the same route that morning reads 17 minutes. What does this comparison tell the planner?

options.text: The model is wrong and must be discarded because one trace disagrees
options.misconception: treats a single discrepancy as proof the model is useless

options.text: The model under-predicts this trip by 3 minutes and warrants a check
The GPS trace is wrong because handhelds cannot time peak traffic
options.misconception: assumes any handheld reading is automatically faulty

options.text: The two numbers are equivalent once rounding to whole minutes
options.misconception: treats a three-minute gap as mere rounding noise

questions.explanation: The model under-predicts by 3 minutes, which is a flag for checking rather than a verdict. A single trace may reflect an unusual day, so the model is not abandoned.
questions.hint: Compare the two numbers and describe the gap.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a correlation in the data from evidence of causation
questions.stem: On the planner's board, lanes with more bus services also show lower average delays, and a colleague concludes that adding buses causes the lower delays. What weakens this causal claim?

options.text: The lanes with the most buses also lie on the widest, least congested roads
options.misconception: misses that road width confounds the service and delay link

options.text: Delay figures for every corridor were recorded by the same two staff
options.misconception: assumes one recording team must mean the data are wrong

options.text: Bus service rose fastest on routes that were already losing passengers
Peak delay and service frequency were both logged for eleven years
options.misconception: treats a long record as evidence of a causal link

questions.explanation: Services grew fastest where ridership was already falling, so both variables track an underlying decline. The association does not isolate bus service as the cause.
questions.hint: Look for a third variable that moves with both.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise bias introduced by where an instrument is placed
questions.stem: A board diagram shows a loop counter whose sensor sits 4 metres above the platform, plus a handheld tally kept by a volunteer. Which measurement bias does the raised sensor introduce?

options.text: It counts only passengers who wait, because the beam is fixed to a doorway
options.misconception: confuses a mounting choice with selective counting

options.text: It undercounts because a loop sensor cannot detect a stationary crowd
options.misconception: believes sensors cannot register people who are not moving

options.text: It overcounts because the 4 metre height doubles the sensed area
options.misconception: assumes greater sensor height always increases the count

options.text: It misses short children, since a beam at that height passes over them

questions.explanation: A beam at 4 metres passes above small children's heads, so they are never counted. The bias comes from where the instrument sits, not from crowding.

questions.learningObjective: Judge a spreadsheet that treats compounded growth as simple addition
questions.stem: A planner's spreadsheet cuts a bus corridor's operating cost by 8 percent each year from a starting 250000 per year. What is wrong with the spreadsheet's third-year figure?

options.text: It adds the three 8 percent cuts to 24 percent off the base
options.misconception: adds percentage cuts instead of compounding them

options.text: It assumes costs fall by a different amount in each of the three years
options.misconception: believes proportional cuts produce constant absolute savings

options.text: It multiplies the base by 0.92 three times, which is the correct method
It adds each year's saving back to the starting figure
options.misconception: adds the saving back instead of scaling the base

questions.explanation: Three cuts leave 0.92 cubed, about 0.7787, of the base, so year three costs near 194700. Adding the percentages to 24 percent would give 190000, the classic linear error.
questions.hint: Scale the base by the remaining fraction each year.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a check of a straight-line projection
questions.stem: A planner extends a flat 6 percent annual rise in bus patronage straight to 2035 without testing it. Propose how the board could test whether that straight-line projection is safe to publish.

answer.exemplar: Reconstruct the patronage series for the last ten years, plot it against year, and compare the observed growth rate with the flat 6 percent used in the projection; then extend the series three more years using the actual trend, including any change in slope, and check whether the straight-line series stays inside the range of plausible growth. If growth is slowing, the projection should curve and be revised before publication.

questions.explanation: A straight-line projection assumes a stable slope. Rebuilding the series and extending it with the observed trend shows whether that slope holds, so any flattening enters the published figures.
questions.hint: Compare the fitted slope with the slope used.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Limits to growth and the limiting factor
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a limiting factor sets a ceiling on growth
questions.stem: On the planner's board, a note reads that the new bus corridor can add only six vehicles an hour because the terminal layover area has room for nine. Explain how this constraint shapes further growth.

answer.exemplar: The layover area sets the ceiling: once nine vehicles are in the layover area at any moment, extra buses cannot be turned around and re-entered into service, so the corridor cannot add vehicles beyond roughly nine per hour of layover capacity regardless of demand, funding or driver numbers. Because this resource cannot be expanded quickly, other investments in the corridor will produce no additional service until the layover area is enlarged or redeployed.

questions.explanation: The layover area binds before demand or funding do, so it sets the ceiling on service. Other inputs can be increased without effect, which means the layover area must be enlarged first.
questions.hint: Name the resource that is fully used first.

questions.learningObjective: Count the days that remain after a mechanism is falsified
questions.stem: A planner's note proposes that signal timing causes the morning delay and states that the mechanism would be falsified if jitter exceeds 15 seconds on any eligible day. Over 24 eligible days, jitter exceeded 15 seconds on 5 days. How many eligible days remain in which the mechanism was not falsified?
questions.explanation: Only days meeting the stated failure condition count against the mechanism, so 5 of 24 days falsify it and 19 remain unfalsified. Days below the threshold support it rather than count against it.
questions.hint: Subtract the falsifying days from the eligible days.

questions.learningObjective: Separate instrument bias from observer bias in a measurement plan

options.text: Compare counts from two different volunteers on the same platform
options.misconception: varies the observer but leaves the instrument fixed

options.text: Compare the automatic counter against a reference count on the same hour

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose a calculation that adds percentages instead of compounding
questions.stem: A planner calculates that a patronage series growing 10 percent then 10 percent ends 20 percent above its start, and repeats that logic for a third year of 10 percent. What is wrong with this calculation?

options.text: Each year's rise applies to the new total, so the three percentages compound
The percentages were applied to the wrong years, so the series is misdated
options.misconception: blames the year labels rather than the arithmetic

options.text: The series was never allowed to grow at all, so it cannot rise
options.misconception: misreads the calculation as a claim of no growth

options.text: Percentages should have been applied to the final total rather than each year
options.misconception: shifts the base so the calculation cannot compound

questions.explanation: Each 10 percent rise applies to a base that has already grown, so the three years together give a factor of 1.331, a rise of 33.1 percent. Adding the percentages treats compound growth as if it were simple interest.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a straight-line graph misleads about future growth
questions.stem: A board diagram shows bus patronage plotted against year, with the historical points curving upwards more steeply than the dashed straight line the planner drew for the future. What does the diagram show?

options.text: Growth is accelerating, so the straight line will understate later years
The straight line is the correct forecast because it matches the first two years
options.misconception: judges a forecast only on its earliest years

options.text: The historical points are wrong, because a straight line is always expected
options.misconception: assumes linearity is a property of the data

options.text: The dashed line will cross the historical data at some future point
options.misconception: expects a projection to intersect the past series

questions.explanation: An upward curve means the slope is increasing, so a straight line drawn from it will fall below the series later and understate patronage. Matching the first two years proves little.
questions.hint: Look at how the slope changes along the curve.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Limits to growth and the limiting factor
questions.learningObjective: Explain a growth ceiling and what would lift it
questions.stem: A bus network adds no new vehicles because the maintenance workshop has capacity for 60 vehicles and already holds 58 in for servicing. Explain what this implies about further growth.

answer.exemplar: The workshop is the binding constraint: with 58 of 60 places occupied, only two vehicles can be added before routine servicing is squeezed, and further additions would mean vehicles off the road for maintenance rather than carrying passengers. Because the workshop was sized for the existing fleet, every other input, including finance and drivers, can be increased with no effect on service. Lifting the ceiling means enlarging the workshop, buying vehicles that need less maintenance, or outsourcing servicing, and each of these should be costed before the network commits to more vehicles.

questions.explanation: Growth stops where the scarcest resource is exhausted, and the workshop at 58 of 60 places is nearly there. More funding or drivers cannot help while servicing capacity binds, so the ceiling must be lifted at the workshop first.
questions.hint: Name the resource that is nearly used up.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A hypothesis and the prediction it makes
questions.learningObjective: Design a test that could confirm or refute a stated hypothesis
questions.stem: A planner's board asks whether a real-time arrival display reduces missed connections at a suburban interchange. Design the comparison the board should run to test that claim.

answer.exemplar: Select comparable weekdays at the interchange, split them into a set with the real-time display operating and a set without, ideally matched on season and service disruption, and compare the proportion of passengers missing a connection in each set. The hypothesis predicts a lower miss rate where displays run, so a difference in the predicted direction across many matched days supports it while no difference, or a difference in the opposite direction, refutes it. Both sets should be measured the same way to avoid instrument bias.

questions.explanation: The claim only means something if the display and no-display days are comparable and the predicted difference can fail to appear. Splitting matched days and measuring both sets identically makes the prediction falsifiable.
questions.hint: Compare like with like on matched days.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain what evidence would be needed to falsify a mechanism
questions.stem: A board note proposes that boarding queues at a terminus are caused by the ticket machine failing twice a day. Explain what evidence would be needed to show this mechanism is not operating.

answer.exemplar: The mechanism predicts that queue length rises shortly after each machine failure and that the pattern repeats on every day the machine fails. The note should therefore be tested by comparing queue lengths in the hours after failures with the same hours on days when the machine did not fail, and by checking whether the two daily peaks coincide with the logged fault times. If queues stay short after failures, or peak at times unrelated to the faults, the proposed mechanism does not account for the observed pattern.

questions.explanation: A mechanism linking cause and effect predicts where and when the effect appears. Comparing post-fault queues with matched fault-free hours, and checking peak times against fault times, tests exactly that.
questions.hint: Look for the predicted timing of the effect.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a check that exposes where a straight-line projection breaks
questions.stem: A board has published a straight-line growth forecast for a bus network through 2040. Design a check that would show where and when the straight line stops being a reasonable description.

answer.exemplar: Take the longest reliable series available for the network and plot annual passenger journeys against year, then calculate the growth rate achieved in each recent year rather than assuming a single constant rate. Extend the observed series forward under the rates it has actually shown, including any slowing in the most recent years, and mark where the straight-line forecast departs from those values by more than the stated uncertainty. The board should also list the assumptions the forecast holds fixed, such as unchanged fares and service levels, so that departures can be attributed to whichever assumption actually moved.

questions.explanation: A straight line can only be judged against a series showing the real slope. Rebuilding the history, projecting it on its own terms and listing held-fixed assumptions shows where the line departs.
questions.hint: Compare the line with the recent slope of the data.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison that can separate a causal claim from a correlation
questions.stem: A board note claims that higher service frequency causes lower car journeys on a corridor. Design a comparison that would test that claim rather than merely repeat the correlation.

answer.exemplar: Compare corridors where service frequency changed with matched corridors where frequency did not, matching on population, road space and existing service so that the only systematic difference is the frequency change. A difference-in-differences reading of before and after journeys, car and bus, in the two groups would estimate the effect of frequency, whereas simply correlating frequency with car journeys across corridors confounds the causal claim with everything else that differs between them.

questions.explanation: A correlation across corridors cannot separate frequency from the many other things that differ between them. A matched comparison of corridors that changed with corridors that did not, read as a difference in differences, can.
questions.hint: Compare groups that differ only in the cause.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how bias enters a measurement and how to limit it
questions.stem: A transit planner's board shows a patronage figure that is consistently 8 percent above the operator's ticket revenue estimate. Explain how this gap could arise from measurement rather than from real demand.

answer.exemplar: The two figures need not be measuring the same thing. If the counter sensor counts passengers who transfer without a fresh ticket, or if the volunteer tally includes staff on the platform, the count will sit above revenue, which only reflects paid boardings. Equally, the gap could run the other way if the sensor under-counts children in pushchairs or misses passengers who board at a rear door. The board should define exactly what is counted before treating either number as the truth.

questions.explanation: A count and revenue can cover different populations, or a device can miss a class of passenger. Stating what each source includes, and checking sensor coverage, separates error from demand.
questions.hint: Ask what each source actually counts.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the conditions that make a linear projection indefensible
questions.stem: A planner plans a new light rail line and has projected a steady 9 percent annual rise in ridership for thirty years. Which feature of the planned system makes that projection least defensible?

options.text: Ridership would depend on new housing and offices that are not yet built
The line runs for 14 kilometres through dense residential districts
options.misconception: reads route length as the reason a projection fails

options.text: The project has a budget of 900 million dollars over six years
options.misconception: treats the budget as evidence about future growth

options.text: The transport authority has promised a review every five years
options.misconception: believes scheduled reviews remove the risk in a projection

questions.explanation: A straight-line projection assumes the conditions that produced recent growth continue unchanged. If ridership depends on developments that do not exist yet, the base the projection rests on has not been fixed, so a constant percentage is unfounded.
questions.hint: Check what future growth depends on.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Limits to growth and the limiting factor
questions.learningObjective: Find the step at which a growth forecast breaks against a constraint
questions.stem: A planner forecasts that adding 8 buses to a corridor will raise daily journeys by 9000, but the terminal layover area already holds nine vehicles and cannot be extended. Where is the forecast most likely to fail?

options.text: At the service step, because the layover area stops the extra buses running
At the vehicle purchase step, because the fleet budget was already spent
options.misconception: blames money rather than the physical constraint

options.text: At the driver step, because nine extra drivers cannot be recruited
options.misconception: assumes the workforce is the first binding limit

options.text: At the counting step, because the survey cannot capture the extra journeys
options.misconception: blames the measurement for the forecast failure

questions.explanation: With the layover area full, the extra buses cannot be turned around and re-entered, so they never run and the extra journeys never appear. Money and drivers are irrelevant while that holds.
questions.hint: Check which resource is already fully used.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A hypothesis and the prediction it makes
questions.learningObjective: Convert a stated percentage prediction into a predicted count
questions.stem: A planner predicts that a 25 percent increase in cycle-boarding follows from the new racks, applied to a baseline of 320 cycle boardings per day. What daily count does the prediction imply?
questions.explanation: A 25 percent increase means multiplying the baseline by 1.25, and 320 times 1.25 is 400 boardings a day. Treating the rise as a share of the new total rather than the old misreads it.
questions.hint: Multiply the baseline by one plus the rate.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a proposed test could actually refute a mechanism
questions.stem: A board proposes to test whether ticket machine faults cause queueing by repairing the machine and noting whether queues shorten. Why is this a weak test of the stated mechanism?

options.text: Because queues could shorten for other reasons, so no result refutes the fault claim
Because the repair changes too many factors to interpret any result
options.misconception: blames the number of factors instead of the missing control

options.text: Because queues cannot be measured accurately enough to detect a change
options.misconception: dismisses the test on measurement grounds without evidence

options.text: Because machines should be repaired regardless of what the queueing shows
options.misconception: treats the service decision as the point of the test

questions.explanation: Repairing the machine removes the fault but leaves other causes running, so any change could come from elsewhere. Without a comparison period the test can neither confirm nor refute the mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask what else could change over the same period.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Select the comparison that gives a fair test of a model
questions.stem: A planner wants to check a demand model against reality. Which comparison gives the fairest test of whether the model's predictions are accurate?

options.text: Compare the model with last year's counts, since those are the same data
options.misconception: reuses model inputs as if they were an independent test

options.text: Compare the model with counts taken on the same day it was last fitted
options.misconception: tests on data the model has already absorbed

options.text: Compare with fresh counts on routes the model never used for fitting
Compare the model with a rival model, and let the more complex one win
options.misconception: judges accuracy by complexity rather than by measurement

questions.explanation: A fair test uses measurements the model has never seen, on routes outside its fitting data, so agreement is real accuracy. Its own inputs or a rival model prove nothing.
questions.hint: Use data the model has never been fitted on.

questions.learningObjective: Read a correlation correctly and identify what it cannot establish
questions.stem: A board note reports that on a corridor with the highest bus frequency, passengers also report the highest satisfaction. What can the planner legitimately conclude from this observation?

options.text: Raising service frequency raises passenger satisfaction
options.misconception: reads a single corridor's pairing as proof of cause

options.text: Satisfaction drives service frequency, since the better-rated corridor got more
options.misconception: reverses the direction of influence on no evidence

options.text: Frequency and satisfaction vary together here, but the cause is not identified
Satisfaction should be funded first, since it is the strongest predictor
options.misconception: treats co-variation as evidence for a funding priority

questions.explanation: The two vary together here, which is a real association, but nothing rules out a third factor such as cleanliness driving both. Direction of influence and the true cause stay open.
questions.hint: Ask what else could move both variables.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a diagram showing two measurement methods disagreeing
questions.stem: A board diagram plots gate counts on one axis against volunteer tallies on the other for 30 minutes of one hour, with the points lying above the one-to-one line. What does the diagram indicate?

options.text: The volunteers counted more passengers than the gate recorded
options.misconception: reads the axes without checking which is which

options.text: The two methods agree, because the points sit close to a straight line
options.misconception: treats linearity as agreement between methods

options.text: The gate under-records relative to the volunteer tally
Passenger numbers rose steadily through the whole measured hour
options.misconception: reads a between-method offset as a time trend

questions.explanation: Points above the one-to-one line mean the tally values exceed the gate values in the same minutes, so the gate records fewer passengers. The offset is a disagreement, not a time trend.
questions.hint: Check which quantity is larger at each point.

questions.stem: A transit board lists fares rising 4 percent in year one, 4 percent in year two and 4 percent in year three from a base of 60 dollars. What fare does that path reach in year three?
questions.explanation: Three increases of 4 percent leave a factor of 1.124864, and 60 times that is about 67.49 dollars. Adding the 4 percent three times to reach 67.20 treats compounding as simple interest.
questions.hint: Apply the growth factor once for each of the three years.

questions.learningObjective: Quantify the gap between a straight-line and a compounding projection
questions.stem: A planner projects daily journeys linearly from 20000 today, adding 1500 per day each year for five years, and separately projects 5 percent annual compounding from the same starting point. What is the gap between the two projected figures in year five?
questions.explanation: Linear gives 20000 plus 5 times 1500, which is 27500, while compounding gives about 25526. The gap of roughly 1974 shows how far a straight line overstates a compounding path.
questions.hint: Compute both projections before comparing them.

questions.topic: Limits to growth and the limiting factor
questions.learningObjective: Bring model, measurement and constraints together in one judgement
questions.stem: A board wants a single recommendation on whether to double bus frequency on a growing corridor. Which package of evidence best supports such a recommendation?

options.text: High passenger satisfaction scores, a rising satisfaction trend and a new logo
options.misconception: treats satisfaction scores as a measure of spare capacity

options.text: A tested demand model, current peak load, and the layover capacity limit
A rising passenger count, a new route map and a positive press report
options.misconception: counts activity rather than testing capacity

options.text: A comparison with two other cities, a league table of fares and a survey
options.misconception: gathers context without measuring the corridor itself

questions.explanation: A sound recommendation needs a tested demand model, the measured peak load and the capacity that bounds any increase. Satisfaction scores and press reports describe mood, not capacity.
questions.hint: Ask what limits the service and how full it runs.

questions.topic: A hypothesis and the prediction it makes
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether results match both the size and direction of a prediction
questions.stem: A planner's board records a prediction that new cycle racks would lift cycle-boarding by 40 per day, and a survey three months later records a lift of 11 per day. What is the proper reading of this comparison?

options.text: The hypothesis is disproved, because the observed lift is smaller than predicted
options.misconception: treats a wrong magnitude as a refutation of the whole claim

options.text: The hypothesis is confirmed, because the count did rise at all
options.misconception: accepts any change in the right direction as confirmation

options.text: The prediction was wrong, because the survey was taken after three months
options.misconception: blames the survey date for a mismatch in size

options.text: The direction matched but the size did not, so the claim needs revision

questions.explanation: The prediction carried both a direction and a size, and only the direction matched. That supports the idea while showing the stated magnitude needs revision, so neither celebration nor dismissal is right.
questions.hint: Compare both the sign and the size of the change.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how far a sample has passed a stated falsification threshold
questions.stem: A planner's note claims that signal priority reduces the average delay on a corridor by 2 minutes, and treats a sampled mean of 13 minutes or more on a corridor with a baseline of 11 minutes as evidence that the claim has failed. A 10-day sample gives a mean of 13.4 minutes. By how many minutes does the sampled mean exceed the threshold for failing?
questions.explanation: The threshold is 13 minutes and the sampled mean is 13.4, an excess of 1.4 minutes. Comparing against the baseline of 11 would give 2.4, which answers a different question about distance from the usual delay.
questions.hint: Subtract the threshold from the sampled mean.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how far a measurement exceeds a model's stated range
questions.stem: A model predicts 1400 bus journeys on a route for a day. The measured total is 1540 and the model's stated uncertainty for such a day is plus or minus 90 journeys. By how many journeys does the measurement exceed the top of the model's range?
questions.explanation: The top of the model's range is 1400 plus 90, that is 1490, and the measured 1540 exceeds it by 50. Comparing with the central estimate of 1400 would give 140, ignoring the stated uncertainty.
questions.hint: Add the uncertainty to the estimate before comparing.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Judge which observation would justify a causal claim
questions.stem: A board wants to know whether a new bus lane reduced car journeys on a parallel road, and must avoid a claim that outruns its evidence. Which finding would justify a causal claim?

options.text: Car journeys on the parallel road fell 12 percent while nearby roads held steady
Bus journeys on the new lane rose 40 percent in the first three months
options.misconception: treats uptake on the new route as evidence about the parallel road

options.text: Drivers reported that the parallel road felt busier after the lane opened
options.misconception: relies on recollection of drivers rather than counted flows

options.text: The lane was approved after a consultation that drew 600 responses
options.misconception: treats consultation volume as evidence about road traffic

questions.explanation: A causal claim needs a contrast with what would have happened anyway. Car journeys falling 12 percent while nearby roads held steady provides it; the other evidence does not.
questions.hint: Look for a matched area that did not change.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Correct a biased measurement by the size of the known bias
questions.stem: A platform loop counter is known to miss 4 percent of passengers because it cannot detect passengers in wheelchairs. On a day it records 5200 boardings, what is the bias-corrected estimate of actual boardings?
questions.explanation: The counter records 96 percent of the truth, so the estimate is 5200 divided by 0.96, about 5417. Adding 4 percent to reach 5408 goes the wrong way, because the gap is a share of the true total.
questions.hint: Divide by the fraction the counter actually catches.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Compounding a proportional change year on year
questions.learningObjective: Explain why repeated proportional changes do not add linearly
questions.stem: A planner notes that passenger numbers rose 6 percent and then 6 percent again, and a colleague announces a 12 percent two-year rise. Why is the colleague's statement wrong?

options.text: Each 6 percent rise applies to a larger base, so two years give about 12.4 percent
Each 6 percent rise applies to a smaller base, so the total is below 12 percent
options.misconception: claims the base shrinks so growth falls behind the sum

options.text: The two rises must be equal because the same percentage was quoted
options.misconception: assumes identical rates must produce identical amounts

options.text: Percentages cannot be added across years at all, so no total can be quoted
options.misconception: overstates the rule against combining percentages

questions.explanation: The second 6 percent applies to a base already 6 percent larger, so the combined factor is 1.1236, a rise of 12.4 percent. Adding the rates to 12 percent slightly understates the compounding.
questions.hint: Multiply the two growth factors together.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Choose the projection method that suits the growth actually observed
questions.stem: A network's patronage has grown at a steady percentage rate for many years and shows no sign of slowing. Which projection method is the most defensible for the board to publish?

options.text: Extend the last three years of change by adding a fixed number each year
options.misconception: uses a constant absolute rise on a compounding base

options.text: Apply the observed percentage rate forward, with the rate stated as an assumption
Extend the single best year on record as if it repeated every year
options.misconception: treats one unusual year as the normal rate

options.text: Hold passenger numbers flat, since every network eventually saturates
options.misconception: assumes saturation is guaranteed regardless of evidence

questions.explanation: A steady percentage rate means compounding from the observed base is what the data support, if the rate is flagged as an assumption. A fixed annual addition misdescribes the record.
questions.hint: Match the method to the growth actually seen.

questions.topic: Limits to growth and the limiting factor
questions.learningObjective: Identify from a dataset the input that is limiting output
questions.stem: A board table lists for each corridor: vehicles funded, drivers hired, platform capacity used, and journeys delivered. Three corridors have spare drivers and funding but sit at full platform capacity. What does the table show?

options.text: Funding is the limiting factor, because funded vehicles set the ceiling
options.misconception: ignores that spare funding cannot be used

options.text: Drivers are the limiting factor, since hired drivers decide the output
options.misconception: ignores that the driver column shows spare staff

options.text: Platform capacity is limiting those three corridors right now
No limit is visible, because every column in the table has a number
options.misconception: mistakes recorded values for evidence of spare capacity

questions.explanation: Where capacity is at its maximum while other inputs stay spare, capacity binds, and more vehicles or drivers would change nothing. Reading a number in every column as spare room reverses the logic.
questions.hint: Look for the column at its maximum while others have room.

options.text: The prediction is wrong, because the points are not on the line
options.misconception: requires exact agreement before accepting a prediction

options.text: The prediction cannot be tested, because the points scatter widely
options.misconception: confuses scatter around a line with an untestable claim

options.text: The prediction is confirmed only if more than half the points sit above
options.misconception: replaces a fair comparison with a majority rule

options.text: The prediction is broadly consistent, with scatter of the expected size

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose a claim that no available test could refute
questions.stem: A board note claims a new timetabling algorithm understands passenger psychology. A test is proposed that runs it for a month and checks whether satisfaction scores rise. Why is this not a valid test of the claim?

options.text: Because satisfaction scores take a month to update after any timetable change
options.misconception: invents a delay in scores to reject the test

options.text: Because the algorithm cannot be used on routes with more than ten services
options.misconception: invents a technical limit to dismiss the test

options.text: Because scores could rise for reasons the claim says nothing about
Because a month is too short for passenger psychology to respond at all
options.misconception: invents a response time to dismiss the test

questions.explanation: A valid test must be able to fail. If satisfaction could rise from cleaner vehicles or lower fares, a rise proves nothing about understanding psychology, and the claim can never be shown wrong.
questions.hint: Ask whether a null result could disprove the claim.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a check separating model error from measurement error
questions.stem: A board's demand model and its manual counts disagree by about 9 percent on several routes. Design a check that would show whether the fault lies in the model or in the counting method.

answer.exemplar: For each of the disagreeing routes, repeat the counts under a stricter protocol that defines exactly who is counted, when a transfer counts as a new boarding and how children in pushchairs are handled, and compare the repeated totals with the original ones. If the repeated counts move towards the model's predictions, the original protocol was the problem; if the repeated counts stay near the originals while the model remains unchanged, the error lies in the model's assumptions about demand or behaviour.

questions.explanation: The sources can disagree because counts are ill-defined or the model misreads demand. Repeating counts under a tightened protocol separates a counting problem from a modelling one before anything is changed.
questions.hint: Redefine and repeat the measurement first.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a correlation is not by itself evidence of causation
questions.stem: A transit board notes that corridors with the most bus shelters also have the highest satisfaction, and drafts a paper saying shelters cause satisfaction. Explain what is missing from that reasoning.

answer.exemplar: The note establishes that two things vary together, not that one produces the other. Corridors with more shelters may also be wider, cleaner, better lit or closer to shops, and any of those could raise satisfaction while the shelters are merely present in the same places. To make the causal claim the board needs an intervention, such as shelters added to matched corridors with none, or a route with shelters added at different times, so that satisfaction is compared with and without the change while the other conditions are held as constant as possible.

questions.explanation: Two variables moving together does not identify which produces which, or rule out a third driving both. The claim needs an intervention so satisfaction is assessed with and without the shelters.
questions.hint: Ask what else differs between those corridors.

questions.hint: Divide the reading by one plus the overcount rate.
